flashcards.front: Name three signs in a login log that an account is under password attack.
flashcards.back_definition: Many failed logins in a short time, logins at unusual hours for that user, and logins from a device or location never seen before.
flashcards.back_example: 47 failures in 90 seconds followed by a success, from an IP the user has never used.
flashcards.back_confusion: One failed login is normal: the rate and the combination of signals matter, not the raw count.
flashcards.back_hook: Too many, too odd a time, too unfamiliar a device.

flashcards.front: Why does a brute-force alert rule use a time window, not just a count?
flashcards.back_definition: The window separates slow human mistakes from fast automated guessing, which cuts false positives.
flashcards.back_example: Rule: 5 failed logins for the same user within 60 seconds.
flashcards.back_confusion: Five failures spread across a week is a forgetful user; five in a minute is a script.

flashcards.front: Brute force vs dictionary attack vs credential stuffing?
flashcards.back_definition: Brute force tries every possible combination. A dictionary attack tries likely passwords from a wordlist. Credential stuffing replays real username and password pairs stolen in another site's breach.
flashcards.back_example: In 2023 attackers stuffed reused passwords into 23andMe, got into 14,601 accounts and through a sharing feature reached data on millions more users.
flashcards.back_confusion: Credential stuffing needs no guessing at all; it works only because people reuse passwords.
flashcards.back_hook: Try everything, try the likely, try the stolen.

flashcards.front: A log shows a success just before the account lockout fired. What does it mean?
flashcards.back_definition: The attacker probably guessed the password before the lockout triggered, so treat the account as compromised: reset it and investigate.
flashcards.back_example: Fail, fail, fail, fail, SUCCESS, then lockout on the next attempt.
flashcards.back_confusion: A lockout stops further guessing; it does not undo a login that already succeeded.
flashcards.back_hook: Locked after the thief got in is still robbed.

flashcards.back_definition: Transformations a cracking tool applies to each wordlist entry (capitalise, swap letters for symbols, append digits) to generate the variants people actually use.
flashcards.back_example: password becomes Password, P@ssw0rd, password1 and PASSWORD!.
flashcards.back_confusion: This is why "add a number and a symbol" does not make a dictionary word safe.
flashcards.back_hook: Attackers already know your clever tricks.

flashcards.back_definition: Length and unpredictability. Each extra character multiplies the search space, and a random multi-word passphrase beats a short complex word.
flashcards.back_example: correct-horse-battery-staple (random words) is far stronger than P@ssw0rd!.
flashcards.back_confusion: Complexity rules that just force symbols give predictable substitutions; length wins on the maths.

flashcards.front: What does NIST SP 800-63B-4 (2025) say about password length and rules?
flashcards.back_definition: At least 15 characters for a password used on its own, 8 when it is part of MFA; allow at least 64; check new passwords against a breached-password blocklist; no forced composition rules and no scheduled expiry.
flashcards.back_example: Change a password only when there is evidence it was compromised.
flashcards.back_confusion: Older advice of 8 characters plus mandatory symbols and 90-day resets is out of date.
flashcards.back_hook: 15 alone, 8 with a buddy, never on a timer.

flashcards.front: What is MFA, and what are the three factor categories?
flashcards.back_definition: Multi-factor authentication requires factors from two or more different categories: something you know (password), something you have (phone, key), something you are (fingerprint).
flashcards.back_example: Password plus a code from an authenticator app.
flashcards.back_confusion: Two passwords, or a password plus a security question, is still only one category: that is not MFA.
flashcards.back_hook: Know, have, are: pick two different ones.

flashcards.front: How does a TOTP code work?
flashcards.back_definition: The app and server share a secret key. Each computes HMAC(secret, time step), where the time step is floor(Unix time / 30), and turns the result into a 6-digit code (RFC 6238).
flashcards.back_example: At Unix time 1700000075 the time step is 56666669.
flashcards.back_confusion: TOTP codes are computed on the device and never travel over the phone network, unlike SMS codes.
flashcards.back_hook: Same secret plus same clock = same code.

flashcards.front: Why is an authenticator app safer than SMS codes?
flashcards.back_definition: SMS codes can be stolen by SIM swapping or number porting, without touching the victim's phone. Authenticator codes are computed locally.
flashcards.back_example: An attacker convinces a phone carrier to move the victim's number to a new SIM and receives their login codes.
flashcards.back_confusion: Both can still be phished in real time by a proxy page; only origin-bound keys or passkeys stop that.
flashcards.back_hook: Your number can be stolen; your app's secret stays home.

flashcards.front: Why do adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits defeat SMS and TOTP MFA?
flashcards.back_definition: The fake page relays the password and the code to the real site in real time and steals the session cookie, which is the real prize.
flashcards.back_example: In 2022 the same SMS phishing campaign breached Twilio but failed at Cloudflare, whose staff used FIDO2 security keys.
flashcards.back_confusion: MFA still blocks password-only attacks; it just is not phishing-resistant unless it is origin-bound.
flashcards.back_hook: Steal the cookie, skip the lock.

flashcards.front: Why should passwords be stored salted and with a slow hash?
flashcards.back_definition: A unique salt makes identical passwords hash differently, defeating precomputed tables. A slow key-stretching function (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2id) makes each guess expensive.
flashcards.back_example: LinkedIn's 2012 leak used unsalted SHA-1, so millions of passwords were cracked within days.
flashcards.back_confusion: Fast hashes such as SHA-256 alone are the wrong tool for passwords: speed helps the attacker.

flashcards.front: How does a password manager reduce account-takeover risk?
flashcards.back_definition: It generates and remembers a unique, random password for every site, so one breach cannot be replayed elsewhere.
flashcards.back_example: Colonial Pipeline (2021) was entered through one old VPN account with a leaked password and no MFA.
flashcards.back_confusion: The vault is encrypted with the master password; pair the manager with MFA, since each covers a different failure.
flashcards.back_hook: One strong lock opens a box of unique keys.
